entry: Difference in form, color or behavior between the sexes of a species. It occurs in most dioecious species, which consist of most animals and some plants. Differences may include secondary sex characteristics, size, weight, color, markings, or behavioral or cognitive traits. Male–male reproductive competition has produced weapons such as "battle" teeth and blunt heads, while passive displays such as ornamental feathering have evolved mainly through sexual selection. The ornate plumage of [[Peafowl|peacocks]] attracts mates but hinders flight and increases vulnerability to predators. In reversed sexual dimorphism, females are larger or more ornamented, as in raptors, [[Spider|spiders]], the leopard seal and certain waders. Sexual dichromatism, a difference in coloration between the sexes, is common in birds and reptiles.

Autoerotic mental image or pattern of thought that stirs sexuality and can create or enhance [[Sexual arousal]]. It may arise from the [[Imagination|imagination]] or [[Memory|memory]], or be triggered by erotic literature, [[Pornography|pornography]], a physical object, or [[Sexual attraction|attraction]] to another person. Sexual fantasies are reported across many societies, but acting them out is far less common because of cultural, social, moral and religious constraints. Fantasies may be positive, negative or both, and they can influence later sexual behavior. Studies usually rely on checklists or written narratives, which depend on retrospective recall.

Sexual fixation on anything not considered sexual by its nature, such as an object, body part or situation. The object of interest is the fetish, and a person who has one is a fetishist. A fetish may be regarded as a [[Mental disorder|mental disorder]] if it causes significant distress or harms important areas of life. Arousal from a particular body part is called partialism, and the DSM-5 merged it into fetishism in 2013. Medical definitions limit the term to objects or body parts, while common usage includes interests such as [[BDSM]] and [[Smoking|smoking]]. In a 1983 review of 48 clinical cases, fetishes most often involved clothing (58.3%), rubber (22.9%) and footwear (14.6%).

Harassment involving unwanted sexual behavior, usually sexual coercion or unwanted advances. It may be verbal, physical or indirect, and it may include sexist remarks, indecent exposure, sexting or [[Sexual assault|sexual assault]]. Harassers and victims may be of any [[Gender|gender]], and all types can harm a victim's physical and mental health. In most countries certain workplace forms are illegal as employment discrimination, though employment laws generally do not prohibit minor isolated incidents. Harassment is often unlawful when it is frequent or severe enough to create a hostile work environment, or when it results in an adverse employment decision such as demotion or firing. Over 100 countries prohibit both hostile environment and quid pro quo harassment. The term was coined in the 1970s, and U.S. lawsuits of that decade and the 1980s shaped its legal meaning.

Type of reproduction involving a life cycle in which two haploid gametes, such as a [[Sperm|sperm]] and an [[Egg cell|egg cell]], fuse to form a zygote with two sets of chromosomes. It is the most common life cycle in multicellular [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], including animals, fungi and plants. It does not occur in [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]] such as [[Bacteria]] and [[Archaea]], though some bacterial gene-transfer processes resemble it. In eukaryotes, [[Meiosis]] produces haploid cells, and genetic recombination increases diversity among offspring. The process is believed to have developed in an ancient eukaryotic ancestor. Its evolution is considered paradoxical, because asexual populations can grow faster; each sexual organism passes on only 50% of its genes. However, sexual reproduction increases genetic diversity and impedes the accumulation of harmful [[Mutation|mutations]].

Social movement that challenged traditional codes of sexual behavior throughout the [[Western world]] from the late 1950s to the early 1970s. It increased acceptance of sexual intercourse outside marriage, aided by the spread of [[Birth control|contraception]], and was followed by wider acceptance of public nudity, pornography, [[Homosexuality|homosexuality]], masturbation and [[Abortion|abortion]]. Influences included Freud's theories of unconscious drives, Mead's ethnographic work on adolescent sexuality in [[Samoa]], and the research of [[Alfred Kinsey]]. By the 1970s premarital and non-marital sex had become increasingly accepted in the United States, with declining stigma around [[Divorce|divorce]]. Critics argue that the movement weakened family structures, while supporters credit it with greater personal freedom and reproductive choice.

Archipelagic country of 115 islands in the [[Indian Ocean]] (pop., 2022: 100,600). Its capital, Victoria, lies about 1,500 km east of mainland [[Africa]], and Seychelles is the smallest country in Africa and its least populated sovereign state. Europeans described the islands in the 16th century, and the voyages of [[Vasco da Gama]] brought them into European knowledge; France formally claimed them in the 18th century, and Britain gained full control in the early 19th century. Independence from the [[United Kingdom]] came in 1976. Since then the economy has shifted from agriculture to service, public sector and tourism activities, and nominal GDP grew nearly 700% from 1976 to 2015. Seychelles belongs to the [[United Nations]], the [[African Union]] and the [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth]].

Class of active galaxy with a quasar-like nucleus. Seyfert galaxies are one of the two largest groups of active galaxies, along with quasar host galaxies. Unlike [[Quasar|quasars]], their host galaxies are clearly detectable. They account for about 10% of all galaxies, and their nuclei are thought to be powered by [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black holes]] surrounded by accretion discs. Seen in visible light most resemble normal spirals, yet their cores can be as luminous as whole galaxies the size of the [[Milky Way]]. The first Seyfert galaxies were detected in 1908 by Edward A. Fath and Vesto Slipher, and [[Edwin Hubble]] classified such objects as extragalactic in 1926. The class is named after Carl Seyfert, who described it in 1943.

entry: Eighth studio album by the English rock band [[The Beatles|the Beatles]], released in the UK on May 26, 1967. Regarded by musicologists as an early concept album, it is considered one of the first art rock LPs and a progenitor of progressive rock. Its styles drew on [[Vaudeville]], circus, music hall, avant-garde, and Western and [[Indian classical music]], and many recordings were colored with sound effects and tape manipulation. The cover, a collage of celebrities and historical figures, was designed by the [[Pop art|pop artists]] Peter Blake and Jann Haworth. The album spent 27 weeks at number one in the United Kingdom. In 1968 it won four [[Grammy Awards]], including Album of the Year, and in 2003 it was inducted into the National Recording Registry of the [[Library of Congress]]. More than 32 million copies had been sold worldwide as of 2011.

Judaism's weekly day of rest, observed from sunset on Friday until nightfall on Saturday. [[Jews|Jews]] refrain from work and rest, remembering the creation of heaven and earth in six days and the Exodus from Egypt. According to [[Halakha]], Shabbat begins a few minutes before sunset on Friday and ends when three stars appear on Saturday night. It begins with candles and blessings over wine and bread, and ends with the Havdalah ritual. Some scholars propose an Akkadian origin in šapattu, a term for the day of the [[Full moon|full moon]].

Fifth Mughal emperor (r. 1628–1658), whose reign marked the zenith of Mughal architecture. The third son of Jahangir, he defeated his brother Shahryar and was crowned in [[Agra|Agra]] Fort after their father's death. He commissioned monuments including the [[Red Fort]] and the [[Taj Mahal]], where his favorite consort, Mumtaz Mahal, is entombed. His campaigns targeted the [[Deccan sultanates]], and he dealt with a devastating Deccan famine of 1630–1632. In September 1657 he named his eldest son Dara Shikoh as successor, which led to a war of succession (1658–1659) won by [[Aurangzeb]]. Aurangzeb imprisoned him in Agra Fort, and after his death he was laid to rest beside his wife in the Taj Mahal.

Indian actor and film producer prominent in Hindi cinema, popularly known as "King Khan." He has appeared in more than 90 films, many of them romantic hits such as *Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge* (1995), *Kuch Kuch Hota Hai* (1998) and *Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna* (2006). He earned acclaim for *Devdas* (2002) and for playing a man with [[Asperger syndrome]] in *My Name Is Khan* (2010). He is co-owner of the [[Indian Premier League]] team Kolkata Knight Riders. He received the Padma Shri from the [[Government of India]], and a National Film Award for *Jawan*.

Epic poem by [[Ferdowsi]], the national epic of Greater Iran. Written between c. 977 and 1010 CE, its some 50,000 couplets make it one of the world's longest epic poems and the longest created by a single author. It tells the mainly mythical but partly historical past of Iran from the creation of the world to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century. Ferdowsi based much of it on a prose work, the Khwadāy-Nāmag, a late [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian]] compilation of the kings of Persia. Traditional historiography holds that it was meant to preserve Persia's golden days for a new generation. Written in Early New Persian, it is central to Persian language and identity, and it is celebrated in [[Iran]], [[Afghanistan]], [[Tajikistan]] and the wider region, including [[Turkey]] and [[Uzbekistan]].

One of the major [[Hinduism|Hindu]] traditions, worshipping [[Shiva]] as the supreme being. Its followers, called Shaivas, number about 385 million, mostly in [[India]], [[Sri Lanka]] and [[Nepal]]. It developed from pre-Aryan religions, Vedic Rudra worship and post-Vedic traditions, absorbing local customs, [[Yoga]] and bhakti. Its earliest sectarian form is the Pasupata movement of the early CE, which spread across North India. Tantric traditions followed, and Shaivism reached Southeast Asia shortly afterward, where thousands of temples were built in Indonesia, Cambodia and Vietnam. It is the Hindu tradition that most accepts ascetic life and emphasizes yoga, encouraging the seeker to discover oneness with Shiva within.

Zulu king (r. 1816–1828), who reorganized the Zulu military into a formidable force. Born at Mthonjaneni in [[KwaZulu-Natal]] Province, South Africa, the illegitimate son of the Zulu king Senzangakhona, he was sent to live with his mother's people and later served as a warrior under Dingiswayo of the Mthethwa. He refined the ibutho regimental system and introduced the short stabbing spear known as the iklwa. He expanded the Zulu Kingdom through war and diplomacy. His reign coincided with the Mfecane (Difaqane), a period of warfare and chaos in southern Africa between 1815 and 1840 that depopulated the region, and his role in it is controversial. He was assassinated by his half-brothers.

Millenarian restorationist Christian sect practicing celibacy and communal living. Founded in England around 1747 as an offshoot of the [[Quakers]], it was known as "Shaking Quakers" for its ecstatic worship. Espousing [[Gender equality|gender equality]], the Shakers practiced [[Celibacy|celibacy]] and [[Pacifism|pacifism]], and they were known for simple architecture, furniture and music. They settled at Watervliet, New York, in 1774. By the mid-19th century 2,000 to 4,000 believers lived in 18 major communities. By 1920 only 12 communities remained in the United States, and since 2019 only one active village, Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village in [[Maine]], has remained.

Collection of 154 [[Sonnet|sonnets]] by [[William Shakespeare]], first published together in a quarto in 1609. They continue the sonnet tradition that began with [[Petrarch]] in Italy, but depart from it by addressing a young man and introducing a Dark Lady. The first 126 are addressed to the young man, and the last 28 are addressed to or refer to a woman. Themes include the passage of time, love, infidelity, jealousy, beauty and mortality. Six additional sonnets appear in plays, including *Romeo and Juliet*, *Henry V* and *Love's Labour's Lost*. The publisher, Thomas Thorpe, entered the book in the Stationers' Register on May 20, 1609. Thirteen copies of the quarto have survived in fairly good shape.

Colombian singer-songwriter, dancer and record producer, known as the "Queen of Latin Music." She is credited with popularizing Spanish-language music worldwide and with opening the international market to other Latin artists. Her first English album, *Laundry Service* (2001), sold over 13 million copies and became the best-selling album by a female Latin artist. Her Spanish-language albums *Fijación Oral, Vol. 1* (2005), *Sale el Sol* (2010) and *El Dorado* (2017) all topped the Billboard Top Latin Albums chart, making her the first woman with number-one albums across four decades. She has won four [[Grammy Awards]] and fifteen Latin Grammy Awards. Involved with the [[FIFA World Cup]] since 2006, she has been described as the tournament's artistic, publicity and humanitarian icon. Her humanitarian work includes the Barefoot Foundation.

Major Hindu denomination in which Shakti, the divine feminine energy, is revered as the ultimate reality. Its supreme goddess is Mahadevi, but the most prominently worshipped deities are [[Durga]], the vanquisher of evil, and [[Kali]], the primal force of time and transformation. Other goddesses include [[Saraswati]], [[Lakshmi]] and [[Parvati]]. Its key scripture, the Devi Mahatmya, is considered as important as the [[Bhagavad Gita]]. Its tantric traditions center on the Mahavidya, a group of ten fierce and esoteric goddesses. The earliest evidence of Shakti worship may be an apparent [[Upper Paleolithic]] shrine at Baghor in [[Madhya Pradesh]], India, dated to between 9000 BC and 8000 BC. Goddess-focused festivals such as Durga Puja are very popular in eastern India.

Sanskrit play by [[Kalidasa|Kālidāsa]], regarded as his best work. Also known as *Abhijnanashakuntalam*, it dramatizes the story of Shakuntala told in the [[Mahabharata]]. Shakuntala is raised in a hermitage, and when King Dushyanta meets her there they marry. A curse from a short-tempered sage causes the king to forget her until she shows him a signet ring he gave her. The ring is lost in a river and later found in the belly of a fish, and the play ends with their reunion. Plots similar to the play appear in earlier texts, including a Buddhist Jataka tale. Its exact date is uncertain, but Kālidāsa is often placed in the 4th century CE.

Fine-grained, clastic sedimentary rock formed from mud of clay minerals and silt-sized particles. Shale splits into thin layers, a property called fissility, and it is the most common sedimentary rock. Its clay minerals are largely [[Kaolinite|kaolinite]], montmorillonite and illite, mixed with [[Quartz|quartz]] grains. A typical shale is about 58% clay minerals and 28% quartz. Red and brown colors reflect iron oxides, while black shale contains more than one percent carbonaceous material. Shales and other mudrocks contain roughly 95 percent of the organic matter in all sedimentary rocks, though in an average shale this is less than one percent by mass.

Unpleasant self-conscious emotion arising from negative self-evaluation against social norms and personal moral standards. It can generate feelings of pain, exposure, powerlessness and worthlessness, which may give rise to [[Anger|anger]], denial, avoidance and a tendency to blame others. Its focus is on the self or identity, in relation to a perceived audience. [[Charles Darwin|Darwin]] described its physical signs, including blushing, downcast eyes and a lowered head, in *The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals*. In individualistic Western contexts shame is often seen as an internal failure of the self, whereas collectivist cultures may treat it as a relational emotion tied to social harmony. Shame is relevant to [[Depression (mood)|depression]], social phobia and some [[Eating disorder|eating disorders]].

Coastal province of East China (pop., 2020: 101.5 million). [[Jinan]] is the capital, while Linyi is the largest city by area and population. Shandong is a pivotal center for [[Taoism]], Chinese Buddhism and [[Confucianism]]. Its [[Mount Tai]] is the most revered mountain of Taoism, and the city of Qufu was the birthplace of [[Confucius]] and later the center of Confucianism. [[Neolithic]] cultures flourished there for millennia. After a period of instability and hardship beginning in the late 19th century, the province has grown rapidly in recent decades. Its economy is China's third-largest provincial economy, with a gross regional product of CN¥10.32 trillion in 2025, an increase of 5.5% on the previous year. It has 153 higher education institutions.

Australian [[Cricket|cricketer]] regarded as the greatest leg spinner in history. He played for Australia from 1992 to 2007 and took 708 Test wickets, a record for any bowler until 2007. He was a member of the Australian team that won the 1999 [[Cricket World Cup]]. Warne captained the Rajasthan Royals to victory in the inaugural season of the [[Indian Premier League]]. He was banned from cricket after testing positive for a prohibited substance, and he was involved in other off-field controversies. He later worked as a commentator and published his autobiography, *No Spin*, in 2018.

Chancellor and reformer of the state of [[Qin dynasty|Qin]] during the [[Warring States period|Warring States]] period. Born in the state of Wey, he migrated to Wei and took office in Qin in 359 BC, becoming its chief minister for twenty years. His reforms strengthened the state's administration, economy and army, laying foundations that enabled Qin to conquer its six rival states. He codified laws and punished those who knew of a crime but failed to report it. Soldiers received land according to battlefield success, and the army was divided into twenty [[Military rank|military ranks]]. [[Han Fei]] credited him with the principles of fixed standards and equality before the law, central to [[Legalism (Chinese philosophy)|Legalism]].
